Sumimi v0.5.4 — **every site gets a file of its own, the tables wear
Umami's names, and the numbers now match Umami's item for item.**

Three changes, and they are one idea: **the storage should not cost the
user anything.** A file per site is faster and lighter; the names are the
reference's, so two datasets can be compared; and the last rule that
differed is now the reference's too, so the comparison comes out equal.

---

## One: one file per site

Until now one database file held the facts of every site. A query for one
site therefore read the whole table's aggregates — and because the traffic
of the sites is interleaved, it read the row groups of *every* site, and the
buffer manager held every site's rows, not just the one being asked about.

⇒ ⇒ Now the **main file** holds the sites and the bookkeeping, and **each
site's facts live in a file of that site's own**, under `<main file>.sites/`.
It is still one instance, one directory, one backup.

**The reason is measured, not argued** (`examples/site_split.rs`, 10 sites ×
1 000 000 rows):

| | one file, all the sites | one file per site, all attached |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| summary | 27.7 ms | **14.4 ms** |
| breakdown | 4.8 ms | **0.6 ms** |
| the buffer manager holds | **211 MB** | **39 MB** |

⇒ ⇒ **The speed comes from the table being per site, not from the instance
being per site** ⇒ ⇒ ⇒ one instance with every site attached is as fast as one
instance per site — **and it keeps one buffer manager**. So there is no
"one instance per site" to operate, and no second process.

**PostgreSQL (the private edition) does not split.** It has an index on
`(website_id, created_at)`, so a database per site would buy almost nothing —
and one database holding every site is exactly Umami's shape.

---

## Two: the tables wear Umami's names

Our fact table was called `event`, and our columns were called `id`, `url`,
`title`, `referrer` and `lifatid`. Umami's are called `website_event`,
`event_id`, `url_path`, `page_title`, `referrer_domain` and `li_fat_id`.

⇒ ⇒ They are now the same names:

| | Umami | Sumimi |
|---|---|---|
| the fact table | `website_event` | **`website_event`** |
| the row's id | `event_id` | **`event_id`** |
| the page | `url_path` | **`url_path`** |
| the page's title | `page_title` | **`page_title`** |
| the referrer's host | `referrer_domain` | **`referrer_domain`** |
| the click id | `li_fat_id` | **`li_fat_id`** |

**A table holds ids, not the rules that made them** — and it holds columns,
not the JSON that filled them. ⇒ ⇒ A row that came from Umami now sits in our
table under the same names, and the two tables can be read as one.

**The API did not change.** The wire still says `url`, `title` and `referrer`;
only the **stored columns** carry the reference's names. The trackers, the
dashboard and every existing integration keep working untouched.

One name still differs: our `channel` is their `referrer_type`. The value
sets match — `direct`, `paidAds`, `referral`, `affiliate`, `sms`, `llm`,
`Search`, `Social`, `email`, `Shopping`, `Video`.

---

## Three: the last rule that differed is now Umami's rule

v0.5.3 renamed the two ids so the tables could be read as one. One rule was
still ours, and it was the only number that came out different when the two
datasets were compared:

> we counted the visitors and the visits over **everything**; Umami counts
> them over the groups that have **at least one page view**.

⇒ ⇒ So a visitor whose only event was a custom event was a visitor for us
and was not one for Umami.

⇒ ⇒ **That is now Umami's rule too.** A visitor who only fired a custom
event is not a visitor, and the visit it was in is not a visit — on both
sides, spelled the same way.

⇒ ⇒ ⇒ **The numbers are equal, item for item.** The one number that used to
differ no longer does.

The page view count, the bounces and the breakdowns were already the
reference's rules, and they did not move.

---

## What this costs

**The migration carries your data over.** This is the first schema change
since v3 that does not throw the rows away. Going from v11 to v12 the facts
move into a file per site and five columns are renamed — and neither of those
changes what a row *means*. ⇒ ⇒ So the rows are **moved, not recomputed**:
each site's rows go into its own file on the first start, with the columns
renamed on the way, and the old file is kept beside the new one as
`data.duckdb.v11.bak` (`data.sqlite.v11.bak` on the SQLite backend).

Both open-source engines do this — DuckDB and SQLite.

Nothing is destroyed, and **no row is recomputed** — the ids, the timestamps and
the values come across as they were.

**A direct query that names the old columns** now has to name the new ones —
`id` is `event_id`, `url` is `url_path`, `title` is `page_title`, `referrer`
is `referrer_domain`, `lifatid` is `li_fat_id`. The reports are unaffected:
they are written once, in the shared layer, and they were updated with the
columns.

**The numbers change in one case**: a visitor whose only event was a custom
event is no longer counted as a visitor, and its visit is no longer counted
as a visit. That is the point of the change — it is what makes the two
datasets comparable.

**A backup is now a directory, not a file.** The instance was always a
directory; the events inside it are no longer one file. The
[self-hosting guide](https://sumimi.dev/self-host/) has an updated script and
an updated restore procedure.
